\chapter{El consejo a otras bibliotecas}
\label{ch:es-consejo}
\hlchaptermodality{473}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can follow advice given to somebody else: hear what a person recommends doing, answer a question that asks the same thing with a different verb, and say that something has to be in good condition.}

Read the librarian's advice to anyone copying the scheme, then answer a question that swaps the verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aconsejar]{aconsejar — to advise}

\label{lesson:ES-C473-aconsejar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el consejo} and \textbf{la biblioteca}. You have the noun. Today you get the verb that goes with it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aconsejar}
\textbf{aconsejar} — to advise.

\begin{quote}
¿Qué \textbf{aconseja} a otras bibliotecas?
\end{quote}

\emph{Aconsejar a alguien} — to advise somebody. \emph{Aconsejar hacer algo} — to advise doing something. \emph{Te aconsejo esperar} — I advise you to wait.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same machine, a different part fed into it}]
Acercarse gave you this pattern outright — \textbf{a-} plus a word plus \textbf{-ar}, \emph{to make it that} — with \emph{acercar} from \emph{cerca}, \emph{alejar} from \emph{lejos}, \emph{aclarar} from \emph{claro}.

Look at what those three have in common. Every one is built on a \textbf{preposition or an adjective}. This word is not:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{built on} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
an adjective or preposition & aclarar, acercar \\
a \textbf{noun} & \textbf{aconsejar}, acompañar \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same machine, different raw material. \emph{Acercar} makes something near; \emph{aconsejar} does not make anything \emph{consejo} — it \textbf{gives} one. So with a noun the sense shifts from \emph{make it that} to \emph{supply that}, which is worth knowing before you try to build your own.

Note the person goes in with \textbf{a}: \emph{aconsejar \textbf{a} otras bibliotecas}. The advice itself follows with no preposition at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{El consejo} already traced it: Latin \textbf{consilium}, a deliberation — from \textbf{con-}, together, and a root about \textbf{calling} or taking counsel.

So advising is, underneath, a \textbf{sitting together}: the word does not mean telling somebody what to do. English keeps the same sense in \textbf{counsel} and \textbf{council}, which are the same Latin word split into two spellings, one for the advice and one for the people giving it.

That is a distinction English had to invent twice. Spanish does it with one noun and one verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what does he advise other libraries
  \item I advise you to wait
  \item the noun this verb was built from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To advise? (\textbf{Aconsejar}.) Built from? (\textbf{El consejo}, with \emph{a-} on the front.) What does \emph{consilium} mean underneath? (\textbf{A sitting together}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[recomendar]{recomendar — to recommend}

\label{lesson:ES-C473-recomendar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{aconsejar} and \textbf{pensar}. The first gives today's meaning, the second gives today's spelling problem.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: recomendar}
\textbf{recomendar} — to recommend.

\begin{quote}
Les \textbf{recomienda} empezar con pocos objetos.
\end{quote}

\emph{Te recomiendo este} — I recommend this one. \emph{¿Qué me recomienda?} — what do you recommend? That last one is what you say to a waiter, and it is the most useful sentence in the lesson.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the e that breaks, and the twin it works beside}]
You said \emph{recomienda}, not \emph{recomenda}. That is pensar's rule: under stress the \textbf{e} breaks open into \textbf{ie}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{stress on the stem} & \textbf{stress on the ending} \\
\midrule
recom\textbf{ie}ndo, recom\textbf{ie}ndas & recomend\textbf{a}mos \\
recom\textbf{ie}nda, recom\textbf{ie}ndan & recomend\textbf{á}is \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only the \textbf{second} e breaks — the one that carries the stress. The first stays put, which is why the infinitive keeps both.

And the twin. \emph{Aconsejar} and \emph{recomendar} overlap almost completely, with one lean:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{what it leans toward} \\
\midrule
\textbf{aconsejar} & what would be wise for you \\
\textbf{recomendar} & what is good, of its kind \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You \emph{recomiendas} a restaurant. You \emph{aconsejas} somebody to rest. Either verb will be understood in either sentence, and a careful speaker picks.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{re-} plus \textbf{commendare}: \textbf{com-}, wholly, plus \textbf{mandare}, to \textbf{entrust} — to put a thing into somebody's hand.

So recommending is not praising. It is \textbf{handing over}: you put the thing in the other person's care and let them judge it.

That \emph{mandare} is busy in English — \textbf{command}, \textbf{mandate}, \textbf{demand}, \textbf{commend} — and the hand inside it is \emph{manus}, the same hand you met in \textbf{el mango}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what do you recommend?
  \item he recommends starting with few objects
  \item which of the two verbs you would use about a restaurant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To recommend? (\textbf{Recomendar}.) I recommend? (\textbf{Recomiendo} — the second e breaks.) What does \emph{mandare} mean? (\textbf{To entrust} — to put in the hand.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el estado]{el estado — the condition}

\label{lesson:ES-C473-estado}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{estar} and \textbf{recomendar}. What somebody recommends often depends on the thing's condition — and the word for that is hiding inside \emph{estar}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el estado}
\textbf{el estado} — the state, the condition.

\begin{quote}
Aceptar solo lo que esté en buen \textbf{estado}.
\end{quote}

\textbf{En buen estado} — in good condition. \textbf{En mal estado} — in bad condition, and of food it means gone off. These two phrases are the word's everyday work.

You have read one of them already, on a donation notice: \emph{juguetes en buen estado}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a participle hardened into a noun, again}]
\emph{Estado} is also the past participle of \emph{estar} — \emph{he estado aquí} — and that is worth being exact about, because the two are not quite the same story.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{where the noun came from} \\
\midrule
el pedido & the participle of \emph{pedir}, hardened \\
\textbf{el estado} & Latin \emph{status}, borrowed as a noun \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

El pedido really is its verb's participle put to work. \emph{El estado} arrived as a noun already, from Latin, and only \textbf{looks} like the participle because both descend from the same verb. The shape coincides; the route does not.

File it with them anyway — the family is the easiest place to remember it — but do not tell yourself you derived it.

Which is why it is \emph{estar} and never \emph{ser} underneath. A condition is temporary by definition, and the word carries that in its bones.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{status}, from \textbf{stare}, to stand — the root \emph{estar} itself came from.

English took \emph{status} whole, and took the rest of the family too: \textbf{statue}, something made to stand; \textbf{station}, a standing-place; \textbf{stable}, able to stand; \textbf{estate} and \textbf{state}, which is the same word arriving twice by different roads.

So \emph{el estado} is a standing — and the political \textbf{State} is that word again, meaning the way a country stands. Spanish uses one noun for both, and a capital letter does the separating.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item accept only what is in good condition
  \item this milk is off, using \emph{estado}
  \item which verb \emph{estado} is the participle of
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The condition? (\textbf{El estado}.) In good condition? (\textbf{En buen estado}.) Which verb is it the participle of? (\textbf{Estar} — Latin \emph{stare}, to stand.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(aconsejar, recomendar, el estado)]{(aconsejar, recomendar, el estado) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R473-repaso-consejo}



\begin{quote}
Three words, no prompts. What somebody does when asked, what they do about a restaurant, and the thing an object has to be in before anyone will take it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the three, cold}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
to advise & \textbf{aconsejar} \\
to recommend & \textbf{recomendar} \\
the condition & \textbf{el estado} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: none of the three was really new}]
Each one is a word you held, put through a machine you had already been shown.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word you had} & \textbf{what happened to it} \\
\midrule
el consejo & \emph{a-} on the front, \emph{-ar} on the end \\
estar & its Latin root borrowed back as a noun \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Acercarse} gave the first machine. \emph{El estado} is the subtler case: it looks like \emph{estar}'s participle and is not derived from it — both come down from Latin \emph{stare}, and the noun was borrowed from \emph{status} directly.

\emph{Recomendar} is the odd one out: its pieces are Latin rather than Spanish, and what you already held was the \textbf{rule for its stem} — \emph{pensar}'s e breaking into ie.

So the chapter asked you to recognise three shapes rather than memorise three words.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Two of the three carry a picture that is still readable.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{underneath} \\
\midrule
recomendar & \emph{mandare}, to \textbf{entrust} — to put in the hand \\
el estado & \emph{stare}, to \textbf{stand} — how a thing is standing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And \emph{aconsejar} is \emph{consilium}, a \textbf{sitting together} — so none of the three is really about giving orders. Advice hands a thing over, or sits down beside you, and neither pushes.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what do you recommend?
  \item he advises accepting only what is in good condition
  \item which of the three is a participle turned into a noun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To advise? (\textbf{Aconsejar}.) To recommend? (\textbf{Recomendar}.) The condition? (\textbf{El estado}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(el consejo a otras bibliotecas) — read it, then answer}

\label{lesson:ES-C473-sintesis-consejo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{aconsejar} and \textbf{en buen estado}. The question below uses the first and the answer uses the second.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
The library that lends objects, asked what others should do:

\begin{quote}
A quien pregunta, le \textbf{recomienda} empezar con pocos objetos, aceptar solo lo que esté en buen \textbf{estado} y explicar muy bien las normas desde el primer día.
\end{quote}

Three pieces of advice, joined by commas and a final \textbf{y}. Spanish lists like this without repeating the verb, so \emph{recomienda} governs all three infinitives: \emph{empezar}, \emph{aceptar}, \emph{explicar}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the question will not use the paragraph's verb}]
This is the thing to carry away. The text says \emph{recomienda}. The question says:

\begin{quote}
¿Qué \textbf{aconseja} a otras bibliotecas?
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the text} & \textbf{the question} \\
\midrule
\textbf{recomienda} empezar & ¿qué \textbf{aconseja}? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Nothing has changed except the verb, and an exam does this on purpose: it checks that you hold the \textbf{meaning} rather than the word. If you learned \emph{recomendar} and not \emph{aconsejar}, the question looks like it is about something else.

So treat the two as one idea with two surfaces, and read past the swap.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say all three pieces of advice, keeping one verb and three infinitives the way the text does.

Now answer the question as asked — starting \emph{Les aconseja…} — and notice you are saying the same thing with the other verb.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the text's verb say? (\textbf{Recomienda}.) What does the question's verb say? (\textbf{Aconseja}.) What must the objects be? (\textbf{En buen estado}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
